extraction.name: Vibravox
extraction.description: A dataset of French speech captured with body-conduction audio sensors containing 45 hours per sensor of speech samples and physiological sounds recorded by 188 participants under different acoustic conditions imposed by a high order ambisonics 3D spatializer. Annotations about the recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions are also included.
extraction.creator: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poirée, Véronique Zimpfer, and Éric Bavu
extraction.publisher: Conservatoire national des arts et métiers (Cnam) and French-German Research Institute of Saint-Louis (ISL)
extraction.citeAs: J. Hauret, M. Olivier, C. Langrenne, S. Poirée, and É. Bavu, “vibravox (revision 071945b),” 2024. [Online]. Available: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Cnam-LMSSC/vibravox
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The recording process consists of four steps performed consecutively for each participant: speech-clean (reading sentences for 15 minutes), speechless-noisy (silent in noisy environment for 2m24s), speechless-clean (silent in quiet for 54s), and speech-noisy (reading in noisy environment for 54s). Recordings were made using five body-conduction audio sensors and one airborne microphone in a 3D sound spatializer.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Out of 200 participants, 188 were retained, with a total of 28,471 sentences (6% of participants and 6.8% of pronounced sentences excluded). Missing data was due to mispronounced sentences, sensors shifting from initial positions, occasional sensor malfunctions, or instances where a microphone was inadvertently left unequipped.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Audio recordings from five body-conduction audio sensors (in-ear microphones, bone conduction vibration pickups, laryngophone) and an airborne microphone. Text sourced from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice. Noise excerpts sourced from Audio Set and in-house ambisonic recordings of concerts and street events.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Voice Activity Detection (VAD) timestamps were extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides. In rare cases where adjusted timestamps exceeded original audio boundaries, the audio was trimmed by 15 ms on the affected side.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A 20 Hz high-pass filter was uniformly applied to each acquisition channel. Post-processing involved three automatic filters: 1) Discarding samples with Phoneme Error Rate (PER) > 10%; 2) Discarding samples with SNR (ratio of speech to silence energy) <= 1.5 dB; 3) Discarding samples where speech energy level (Lspeech_50) was not greater than silence energy level (Lsilence_50).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Linguistic transcriptions were derived from the text read by participants (French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice), filtered to exclude proper names, numbers, Greek letters, mathematical symbols, or syntactic errors. Text was normalized (lowercased, punctuation removed except apostrophes). Phonetic transcriptions were generated using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) via the text phonemizer of the CoML lab, with manual correction for unrecognized words.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Phoneme Error Rate (PER) was computed using the Levenshtein distance between the labeled phonetic transcription and the phonetic transcription derived from Whisper's output to ensure high-quality labels (filtering out PER > 10%).
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: 188 participants (97 Female, 91 Male). Age: Mean 28.55 years, Median 25 years, Min 18 years, Max 82 years. A deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group of participants.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: whisper-timestamped model, text phonemizer of the CoML lab
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Available online on HuggingFace. Revision 071945b mentioned.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Audio recordings of voice and physiological sounds (heart rate, breathing), biometric information (skull and timbre uniqueness), age, gender.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Potential advantages in noisy environments (military, industrial). Applications in access control, intelligence gathering, and battlefield forensics. Could improve communication for individuals in high-noise professions.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Lombard effect causes speakers to increase vocal effort in noisy conditions, meaning reported signal-to-external-noise ratios are a lower bound. In-ear microphones may have inadequate acoustic sealing for certain ear canal anatomies due to the 'one-size-fits-all' design.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Limited bandwidth of speech captured by body-conduction sensors due to inherent low-pass filtering of tissues. Inability to capture high-frequency phonemes (e.g., voiceless alveolar and plosive fricatives). Acoustic sealing issues with in-ear microphones for certain anatomies. Sensor sensitivity drift or malfunction in some recordings.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation for Speech Enhancement (Bandwidth Extension), Speech Recognition (Speech-to-Phonemes), and Speaker Verification.
